Michael Burry, the investor who famously predicted the 2008 housing market crash, is back in the spotlight as a sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks draws renewed attention to his warnings about a potential AI bubble.

The investor has become increasingly vocal on X as major AI names, including Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius, have suffered steep declines. On November 19, Burry declared, "Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all." He said he had not necessarily recommended shorting those stocks but had provided investors with information that could justify selling them.

His warnings were not entirely new. In September, Burry raised concerns that expensive AI chips could lose economic value faster than companies recognize through depreciation. In October, he highlighted the financial pressure facing CoreWeave as borrowing costs increased. According to Business Insider, he also urged Nvidia shareholders to get out of the stock in a November 11 Substack post and warned about risks facing AI infrastructure providers the following day.

The selloff has been dramatic. As of November 19, CoreWeave and Nebius had fallen approximately 76% and 66%, respectively, from their earlier highs, while Nvidia was down about 39% from its October peak. Those declines have added credibility to Burry's concerns, although they do not establish that the broader AI bubble has burst. ChatGPT holds Nebius in a live trading experiment and disagreed with Burry on the stock in August. Read the argument.

But while Burry has been bearish on some of the biggest names in artificial intelligence, he has not abandoned the stock market. His latest reported trades reveal that he has been buying shares of companies across technology, e-commerce, healthcare, and other industries, even as markets struggle. In August, he was long a beaten-down healthcare stock, an animal health company that had dropped more than 70% from its 2021 peak.

So, if Michael Burry is betting against parts of the AI boom, what stocks is he buying instead? Click to see the full list of 10 stocks in Michael Burry's updated portfolio as of this month.

Methodology

For this article, we reviewed Michael Burry's publicly accessible commentary on his Cassandra Unchained Substack, financial news reports covering his November 2026 trading disclosures, and portfolio information published by third-party tracking accounts.

Burry's former investment firm, Scion Asset Management, deregistered with the Securities and Exchange Commission in November 2025, as Reuters reported. Consequently, a current comprehensive 13F filing is not available to establish his exact portfolio composition, position sizes, or holdings rankings.

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI continues to show strong marketplace momentum in Argentina despite challenging consumer spending conditions. In the third quarter of 2026, gross merchandise volume (GMV) increased 40% year over year on a foreign-exchange-neutral basis, while items sold grew 19%. The performance reflects the company's ability to attract spending from physical retail even as overall consumption remains subdued.

A key factor supporting this momentum is MercadoLibre's expanded free-shipping offering. In September, the company extended free and fast shipping on lower-priced products for MELI+ members across all delivery methods within its managed network compared with fulfillment-only coverage previously. This made the vast majority of products eligible for shipping benefits. As a result, free-shipping penetration reached levels comparable to Brazil and Mexico, while purchase frequency touched a record high in September.

Growth accelerated most in Argentina's interior regions, where online shopping remains less developed than in Buenos Aires. MELI+ members are also purchasing mid- to higher-priced products more frequently, suggesting that engagement is expanding beyond cheaper purchases.

Stronger shopping frequency and wider shipping coverage could help MercadoLibre maintain its growth momentum in the future. However, weak consumption and the additional cost of shipping benefits remain challenges. Management expects the near-term margin impact to be limited, given the program's focus on MELI+ members.

How Does MercadoLibre Stack Up Against Its Industry?

MercadoLibre, which competes with Amazon.com, Inc. AMZN and Sea Limited SE, has seen its shares tumble 30.5% over the past three months compared with the industry's 10.2% decline. While Amazon shares have fallen 5.9%, Sea Limited has plunged 45.9% in the aforementioned period.

The consensus estimate for MercadoLibre's current fiscal-year sales indicates year-over-year growth of 44.6%, while the consensus estimate for earnings per share suggests a 6.8% decline. For the next fiscal year, the consensus estimates project sales and earnings growth of 29.2% and 39.5%, respectively.

Key Takeaways

Bank of America cut its MercadoLibre price target to $2,000 from $2,400 on Nov. 19 and kept its Buy rating, 48% above the Nov. 20 close.

MercadoLibre is giving up margin to stay ahead of rivals, including Sea Limited's Shopee in Brazil and Nu Holdings in credit.

On 2028 earnings estimates, $2,000 is 27x, below any forward multiple the stock has traded at in five years.

The valuation looks fair, but estimates keep falling, so $2,000 will likely take more than 12 months to reach.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) stock has lost 29% in a year, closing at $1,355.00 on Nov. 20. On Nov. 19, Bank of America cut its price target to $2,000 from $2,400 and kept its Buy rating, 48% above that close. The bank also lowered its 2026 to 2028 EPS estimates, saying the company is putting off monetization to reinvest in its lead.

MercadoLibre is spending heavily against two well-funded rivals: Sea Limited (SE:NYSE)'s Shopee in Brazil, and Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE) in credit.

A margin MercadoLibre chose to give up

Sea can afford the fight. Shopee's adjusted EBITDA rose 44.7% to $269.2 million in the third quarter, its most profitable quarter ever. Sea CEO Forrest Li said Brazil remained Shopee's fastest-growing market, and its new instant delivery service there already delivers in under four hours from more than 7,000 partner stores.

MercadoLibre's Nov. 4 report showed the cost of keeping up. Revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but GAAP operating income fell 6.6% to $676 million. That's a 6.3% margin, against 9.8% a year earlier. Management tied the drop to more free shipping, nearly 20% more fulfillment space added from the prior quarter ahead of peak season, and heavier affiliate marketing in Brazil.

Bank of America is betting on the card

Analyst Robert Ford Aguilar has made Mercado Pago's credit card a big part of his case. In a June note, he forecast a $443 million EBIT loss on the card in 2026, breakeven in 2028 and $1.5 billion of EBIT by 2030. He put MercadoLibre's share of Brazil's card balances at 3.4% in March. Nu's credit portfolio rose 33% in a year, FX-neutral, while MercadoLibre's rose 62%, to almost $18 billion.

Many investors, seeing such a big drop in a stock's price, will steer clear, assuming there's trouble afoot. Others will take a closer look to see if the lower price is actually an enticing opportunity.

MercadoLibre is home to both a dominant online marketplace (Mercado Libre) and a major fintech business (Mercado Pago), both focused on the Latin American market. It's active in 18 countries and was recently delivering 3.2 billion items annually. It sports 136 million unique buyers and 93 million monthly active users (both numbers as of the third quarter). And it's growing briskly, with net revenue recently up about tenfold since 2020.

So what's going on that would depress the stock? Well, there are some concerns, such as:

Competition has been growing in the fintech realm.

The e-commerce side of the business is potentially facing more competition, too, from outside retail giants.

Geopolitical tensions in Latin America, such as in Brazil, might destabilize the business -- as the more business-friendly candidate didn't win the presidential election.

Profit margins have been shrinking.

Those are legitimate concerns, but they aren't deal-breakers. As MercadoLibre notes, it has built a powerful ecosystem, combining "the region's largest e-commerce platform, its fastest and most reliable logistics network, one of its biggest digital banks, its largest fintech payments processor, and a top-3 digital ads platform -- with a loyalty scheme that ties it all together." That's not easy to compete against.

Meanwhile, the shrinking profit margins are partly due to the company extending more free shipping and credit to shoppers and investing in future growth, such as by expanding its fulfillment capabilities. If I weren't already a shareholder, I'd consider MercadoLibre for my portfolio.

title: Can MercadoLibre's GMV Growth Fuel Long-Term Earnings Gains?
detail:
Can MercadoLibre's GMV Growth Fuel Long-Term Earnings Gains?
Sumit Singh
November 16, 2026 4 min read
MELI
AMZN
SE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI continues to build momentum in Latin America's e-commerce market, supported by higher purchase frequency, expanding customer engagement and improving logistics efficiency. In third-quarter 2026, gross merchandise volume (GMV) reached $22.8 billion, increasing 38% year over year on a reported basis and 33% on an FX-neutral basis, while items sold rose 36% to 867 million. Unique active buyers increased approximately 22.3% to 93.9 million, highlighting sustained marketplace adoption and deeper customer engagement.

Brazil remains a major growth driver, with FX-neutral GMV advancing 36% and items sold rising 45%. The company's lower free-shipping threshold continues to encourage more frequent purchases, with items per buyer increasing 16% year over year. Management also reported stronger retention among customer cohorts acquired after the threshold reduction. However, smaller baskets and more free shipments have reduced shipping revenue per shipment. As a result, net shipping margin as a percentage of GMV has declined approximately 200 basis points since first-quarter 2025.

Meanwhile, Brazil's cost per shipment fell 5% year over year in local currency and 14% compared with first-quarter 2025, reflecting improving logistics efficiency. In September, free and slow shipments in the R$19-R$79 price range became variable contribution-positive for the first time. MercadoLibre is also expanding its logistics capabilities, having opened 13 Metro fulfillment centers over the past 12 months and more than doubled the number of sorters and robots across its network. Management expects higher shipment density, automation and better network utilization to drive further cost improvements.

Still, stronger GMV growth has yet to translate fully into operating profitability. Third-quarter operating income declined 6% year over year to $676 million, while the operating margin reached 6.3%, down 40 basis points sequentially. Net shipping costs created a 60-basis-point margin headwind, reflecting increased free shipping, higher energy expenses and additional fulfillment capacity. Increased affiliate marketing investments in Brazil also pressured margins. Nevertheless, net income rose 6% to $448 million, supported by a lower tax rate and reduced foreign-exchange losses.

Management expects improving logistics productivity and greater operating scale to gradually reduce shipping costs relative to business volumes. MercadoLibre's ability to sustain purchase frequency while lowering fulfillment costs remains central to translating marketplace growth into stronger long-term earnings.

MercadoLibre's third-quarter revenue and financial income rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but operating margin declined to 6.3% as shipping, fulfillment, and marketing investments pressured profitability.

Sea Limited (SE) reported 41.3% revenue growth at Shopee in the third quarter, while Nu Holdings (NU) provides another perspective on Brazilian consumer credit conditions.

MercadoLibre appears potentially undervalued following the selloff, although stronger margins and continued market share gains will be important to a sustained recovery.

What Happened?

MercadoLibre (MELI) stock declined approximately 20% from its October 5 closing price of $1,860.61 to $1,490.24 on November 10, after hitting a new 52-week low on November 5.

The decline reflects two concerns: political uncertainty in Brazil and weaker-than-expected profitability despite strong revenue growth.

Brazil's October 25 presidential runoff delivered another term for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who defeated Flávio Bolsonaro after trailing him in the first round.

MercadoLibre shares fell approximately 8% on October 26 as investors reassessed Brazil's economic outlook, currency risks, and consumer spending conditions.

Brazil generated approximately $15.2 billion of MercadoLibre's $28.9 billion in 2025 revenue, making it the company's largest market.

However, the company's third-quarter earnings report created a more immediate concern.

According to MercadoLibre's third-quarter financial results, revenue and financial income increased 45% year over year to $10.75 billion, but reported earnings of $8.83 per share fell short of the $9.27 consensus estimate cited in the initial research brief.

Operating margin declined to 6.3% from approximately 9.8% a year earlier, reflecting higher shipping expenses, expanded fulfillment capacity, and increased marketing spending in Brazil.

In its third-quarter shareholder letter, management described the pressure on shipping margins as "the price of the habit we set out to build."

The strategy is producing results. Items sold in Brazil increased more than 40% year over year for the fifth consecutive quarter, while MercadoLibre gained market share across its three largest markets.

Its lower free-shipping threshold also encouraged smaller purchases, initially putting pressure on shipping economics.

By September, Brazilian orders valued between R$19 and R$79 that qualified for free or slower delivery became variable contribution-positive for the first time, suggesting higher order volumes are beginning to improve shipping economics.

Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre stock fell 10% in the week to Nov. 10 after third-quarter EPS came in at $8.83, short of the $9.27 analysts expected, even as revenue rose 45%.

Management chose the squeeze, spending on free shipping and warehouses while Sea Limited's Shopee keeps gaining in Brazil.

Brazil's cost per shipment is falling, and credit held steady, a bar for Nu Holdings ahead of its expected Nov. 12 report.

Analysts still expect an earnings rebound, and the stock trades far below its usual forward multiple.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) stock fell 10% from Nov. 3 to Nov. 10, with most of the damage in a 12% drop on Nov. 5, the day after its report. Revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, but EPS of $8.83 missed the $9.27 expected.

That spending comes as Shopee, owned by Sea Limited (SE:NYSE), pushes harder in Brazil, which Sea said on Nov. 10 was again its fastest-growing market. And MercadoLibre's credit sets a bar for Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE), which is expected to report on Nov. 12.

The miss was a choice

Operating income fell 6.6% to $676 million, a 6.3% margin against 9.8% a year earlier. The company paid for more free shipping, added fulfillment space ahead of the holidays and stepped up affiliate marketing in Brazil. CEO Ariel Szarfsztejn told analysts the company is spending because the opportunity in front of it is large. "We have accepted a lower margin to do that," he said.

But the shipping bill is starting to shrink: Brazil's cost per shipment fell 5% from a year earlier in local currency. And in September, orders between R19andR79, which now ship free, paid their own variable costs for the first time.

Shopee is pushing just as hard. It launched four-hour delivery in greater São Paulo in August with more than 4,000 partner stores, and Sea said on Nov. 10 that the service now runs from more than 7,000. MercadoLibre began testing one-hour delivery in parts of the city in September. Sea also said Shopee again grew faster than Brazil's broader market in the third quarter.
